title: Transboundary haze — Singapore · Indonesia (2015–16)
description: Between June and October 2015 fires on Indonesian peatland produced the worst haze episode on record. Singapore's 24-hour PSI passed 300 — the hazardous band — schools closed, and regional economic losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars. Singapore had passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in 2014, asserting liability over companies whose activities caused haze in Singapore regardless of where they operated. Indonesia objected to its extraterritorial reach and declined to release plantation concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, citing sovereignty and domestic data law. Indonesia announced a peatland moratorium in late 2015 and established the Peatland Restoration Agency in January 2016. Positions are reconstructed from the public record and are not official; see source note. Source: ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (2002); Singapore Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (2014); Indonesian Presidential Regulation 1/2016 (BRG).

sources.title: ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (2002) — full text
facts: Done at Kuala Lumpur on 10 June 2002; in force from 25 November 2003.
Article 3(1): parties keep the sovereign right to exploit their own resources, with a duty not to cause environmental damage to other states.
Article 8(1): each party's monitoring centre must send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals.
Article 9: parties must control open burning and prevent land clearing using fire.
Article 27: disputes are settled amicably by consultation or negotiation; there is no court or tribunal.

sources.title: Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014 (No. 24 of 2014)
facts: Section 4: the Act extends to conduct outside Singapore.
Section 5(2)(a): a fine of up to S$100,000 for every day of haze pollution in Singapore.
Section 5(2)(b): up to S$50,000 more per day for failing to comply with a preventive measures notice.
Section 5(5): the aggregate fine is capped at S$2 million.
Section 6: anyone in Singapore who suffers injury, property damage or economic loss can sue, whether or not the conduct is actionable abroad.
Section 8: an entity owning or occupying land where a fire burns is presumed to have caused the haze, and ownership can be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government.
